source.title: Cholinergic modulation enables scalable action selection learning in a computational model of the striatum

confidence_rationale: Computational modelling study showing that cholinergic gating in striatum enables channel-specific plasticity, preventing cross-channel interference -- directly relevant to the channel-orthogonality constraint in Q-017. Re-assessed 2026-08-10 while formalizing MECH-142 (control_plane.cholinergic_axis_orthogonality_maintenance): the model's own contrast condition -- global (non-gated) modulation causing 'weight increases not only for the current stimulus, but also for any stimulus previously associated with the same action', i.e. channels drifting toward mutual reinforcement without ACh gating -- maps onto MECH-142's specific mechanism claim (active maintenance required; drift under co-activation without it) more directly than onto Q-017's axis-count question, which is why confidence is raised from the original 0.65. Still a computational model, not REE substrate or empirical multi-loop data.
failure_signatures: Without channel-specific ACh gating, synaptic weights for a given action strengthen regardless of which stimulus triggered reward delivery, so distinct stimulus channels converge poorly due to mutual reinforcement -- the modelled analogue of MECH-142's predicted axis drift under repeated co-activation.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Acetylcholine from striatal cholinergic interneurons acts as a channel-specific gating signal restricting plasticity to post-action temporal windows, suppressing cross-channel interference; direct pathway (D1) neurons maintain stimulus-specific responses while indirect pathway (D2) neurons suppress outdated associations; ACh-gated learning scales well with task complexity (multiple competing stimuli and actions). The paper's own ablation contrast (global vs. channel-specific modulation) shows that removing the gating signal causes cross-channel weight-sharing: reward-triggered strengthening spreads to any stimulus previously paired with the same action, degrading channel separation.
mapping.ree_translation:
Q-017 asks about the minimal orthogonal control-axis subset. This paper provides a mechanistic account of how orthogonality between control channels is actively maintained: cholinergic gating ensures that plasticity in one channel does not bleed into adjacent channels. In REE, the three cortico-striatal loops (sensorium, thought/planning, action commitment) need to maintain orthogonal error signals (MECH-069). ACh-mediated channel specificity is a candidate mechanism for preserving that orthogonality -- if REE's loops shared a common hebbian update without gating, their error signals would become correlated over time, collapsing the independence of the control axes. The scalability finding (ACh gating keeps channels separate even in complex multi-stimulus environments) is directly relevant to Q-017: without active channel segregation, the minimal set of orthogonal axes may not remain minimal under operational conditions.

MECH-142 translation (added 2026-08-10): MECH-142 asserts that valence-arousal axis orthogonality in the control plane 'is not a static geometric property but requires active cholinergic maintenance during learning; without it, axes drift toward correlation under repeated co-activation.' This paper is the direct evidentiary basis for that mechanism claim, not merely an analogy: its own global-vs-gated ablation is precisely a maintenance-vs-no-maintenance contrast, and the failure mode it reports under the no-gating condition (weight sharing/convergence across previously co-activated stimulus channels) is the modelled instance of 'axes drift toward correlation under repeated co-activation.' The residual gap is the same one flagged for Q-017 -- this is plasticity-level channel specificity in a spiking-network striatum model, not a direct demonstration that REE's valence and arousal representations specifically would drift without an analogous gate -- but the mechanism-level match to MECH-142's own wording is tighter than to Q-017's axis-count framing.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This is a spiking neural network model, not empirical data from multi-loop conflict scenarios. The 'channels' in this model are stimulus-action pairs, not REE's qualitatively distinct loop types with incommensurable error signals, and not specifically REE's valence/arousal axes. ACh gating in this model is a plasticity mechanism, not a control-plane axis selection mechanism; the mapping to REE's axis minimality question (Q-017) requires inferring that channel-specific learning also implies channel-specific representation at test time. For MECH-142 specifically, the paper demonstrates the general principle (active gating prevents co-activation-driven drift) in a striatal action-selection context, not in an affective valence/arousal context -- the domain transfer from action-channel plasticity to affective-axis orthogonality is inferred, not directly tested.
mapping.source_context: Computational spiking neural network model of striatum, reinforcement learning tasks with distractors and contingency reversals, no species-specific empirical data

confidence_components.notes: Strong computational result from a biologically-constrained model. For Q-017, the transfer from plasticity-level channel specificity to representation-level axis orthogonality requires an additional inferential step. For MECH-142, mapping_fidelity is raised relative to the original Q-017-only assessment because the paper's own ablation (gated vs. global modulation) is structurally the same contrast MECH-142 predicts (maintenance present vs. absent -> orthogonality preserved vs. drift); the residual risk is domain transfer from striatal action-channels to affective valence/arousal axes, captured in transfer_risk. The Grillner group's involvement (Karolinska) adds credibility to the biological grounding.
